prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a specific invention with a clear identity: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes the light shift that otherwise limits a many-atom optical clock, and the programme then reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. The impact is concrete and already broad: the route to redefining the second, tests of fundamental constants and of relativity through geodesy, and searches for dark matter. It is an invention rather than a lifetime achievement, which is how I understand the physics criterion of a discovery or invention. The attribution is the cleanest on our shortlist. Katori proposed and first realised the concept, and Ye's group drove the record accuracy and the many-body clock work, so two names fit the story without leaving an obvious gap. It has also drawn the broadest support in the opening ballots: it was ranked by all eight of us, including a first place from two colleagues. In my opening ballot I ranked aberration-corrected electron optics (B042) first. After reading the other seven ballots I no longer think I should push it as the preferred configuration, for the reasons given below.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2005 prize to Hall and Haensch for the frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy, together with the ion-clock community around Wineland's earlier recognition. A committee could fairly say precision timekeeping has been rewarded recently and that the lattice clock is a refinement of earlier ideas. The redefinition of the second has also not happened, so the practical payoff is still partly prospective. Priority among Katori, Ye and groups such as Lemonde, Ludlow or the PTB and NIST teams will be argued. I recall the chronology of the first lattice-clock demonstrations from general knowledge and have not verified it against the nomination text. My own preferred field, B042, I place second because its attribution is more complicated than I wrote in the opening ballot. The three credited names omit the scanning-transmission corrector work (Krivanek and collaborators), and no colleague ranked it highly. Some of that is probably because it is a field outside most of the committee, and I cannot rule out that my own closeness misleads me in either direction.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first because progress rests on how accurately we can measure, and he treats the overlap with the earlier frequency-metrology prizes as a possible argument against it, not a decisive one.
responses.response: I agree with the substance and with his two-person split, but I would weigh the overlap more seriously than he does. The 2005 prize recognised the comb and the spectroscopy that make an optical clock countable. The lattice clock is a different invention, because the magic-wavelength trap is what lets one interrogate many atoms without perturbing the transition. If our citation says 'optical lattice clock' and nothing broader, it stays on the right side of that line. I would resist any wording that drifts toward 'optical clocks' in general, since that would reopen the ion-clock question.

responses.point: Lindroth, who ranks the clock first from an atomic-physics view, asks whether the committee wants to separate the lattice-clock concept from the later accuracy race, and notes that priority details are recalled from memory.
responses.response: That is the real allocation question and I think it supports Katori and Ye together rather than weakening it. Katori's proposal gave the concept and the first realisations. Ye's group is the reason the concept became a 1e-18 instrument with controlled systematics, and the credit for the later accuracy race clearly goes to that group. Splitting the two would make a prize for an idea without a demonstrated consequence, or the reverse. I share her caution about priority: I would want the committee file, not our memories, to settle the dates for the first lattice-clock demonstrations before we write the citation.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks topological insulators (B016) first as an unusually complete theory-to-experiment chain, while noting that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are outside the credited names and that the 2016 prize covers neighbouring work.
responses.response: I accept that the theory-experiment chain is strong and that the field is of great importance. My difficulty is the same one he names. The HgTe proposal is the step connecting Kane and Mele's prediction to Molenkamp's observation, and it is not represented in the credited set. With Zhang deceased, the three-name configuration looks incomplete in a way the lattice clock does not. I also think the 2016 overlap is a stronger objection than he allows. I therefore rank B016 below B014, but I do not regard it as a weak candidate and would not object to it as a second part if the credit problem could be resolved.

responses.point: Mehlig supports the lattice clock as clear and concrete with a fair two-person prize, but raises as a fairness issue the relative weight of the ion-clock and lattice-clock communities.
responses.response: I think the fairness issue is real but is answered by the scope of the citation. Ion clocks and lattice clocks share a purpose but not a mechanism, and the Wineland recognition in 2012 was for controlling single quantum systems, not for a many-atom optical standard. I would not widen the prize to cover the ion-clock community, because that would take us beyond three names and blur what is being honoured. I do concede that people in that community will see this as a choice, and the committee text should say so.

responses.point: Johansson ranks topological insulators first and the trapped-ion and neutral-atom work (B008) second, and he flags a possible conflict of interest on circuit QED because of his own research area.
responses.response: I appreciate that he declared the proximity on B009. On B008 my reservation is that it is a compound candidate: ion-trap proposals and experiments together with cold-atom simulation are close to two prizes in one, and the 2012 prize already sits next to it. I would rather award a single sharply defined invention than make a citation that has to cover several programmes. I would be interested in how he would phrase a citation for B008 that does not require the committee to choose between Blatt and Bloch.

uncertainties: Exact priority and chronology of the first magic-wavelength lattice-clock demonstrations, and whether other groups share credit for them.
Whether the committee reads the overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize as disqualifying or as acceptable.
How much weight to give a prospective redefinition of the second that has not yet been decided.
Whether B042 deserves more support than my closeness to the field allows me to judge, and whether Krivanek and the STEM-corrector work make its three credited names incomplete.
statement.conflict_note: For B014 I see no direct personal tie to Katori or Ye from my profile. I hold a University of Tokyo fellowship and have long-running academic exchanges with Japanese universities, and Katori works in Japan, so I flag that as a possible institutional connection to check before I vote on B014 (I do not know whether he is at an institution I am connected to). For B042, which I ranked first and now list as an alternative, I work in electron microscopy, serve as president of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy and know that community, so I should be recused from advocating or voting on it. Johansson is at Chalmers like me, but that affects no shortlisted ballot that I can identify.
